newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures came under pressure on Monday amid widespread selling in European bond markets sparked by uncertainty about European monetary union and nervousness about the chance of a U.S. rate rise next week.
The June contract followed the Bund contract through a series of key support levels. Rolling over of short March positions knocked the contract into the red after a positive, but nervous start.
Traders said it then came under pressure from non-resident sales, notably by U.S. houses, before the U.S. open, sending the contract down to 128.70.

Local traders stepped in to halt the decline but another wave of selling from two more U.S. houses, combined with locals being forced to reverse their positions, sent the contract down to settle 0.98 lower at 128.32.

A trader at German bank said U.S. funds had been cutting positions at the long end in France and Germany to reduce the sensitivity of their portfolios because of the uncertainty surrounding both the next Fed meeting on March 25 and the monetary union process.
He said Monday's move followed a similar lightening of positions by U.S. funds in so-called peripheral European bond markets such as Spain and Italy last week.

Some analysts said they were sceptical as to why concern about the ability of Germany to hit the Maastricht criteria would be weighing on the French market. "There was nothing new (about EMU) from what we had last week, so why are we starting (to sell off) today?" Philippe Brossard at ABN Amro said.
Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch in Paris, said she did not think the selloff on Monday was related to concern about EMU from a French perspective.
"I don't think it's EMU related, if anything we had good news today with Waigel talking about 'fudging' which means there's a better chance of it going ahead," she said.
Some said comments by German Finance minister Theo Waigel that special factors could be taken into account when interpreting Maastrict criteria meant a risk premium should be priced into Bunds.

Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said there was growing uncertainty about the EMU whole process and given that Germany appeared to be at the centre of the problem it was perhaps not such a safe place for investors to be.
"Perhaps the U.S. market is a better place to go given the absolute yield spreads," Lindsay said.

Traders said there was little interest in the cash market from French investors. One trader said domestic investors tended to stay out of the market when it was declining rapidly but there had been some interest at the short end of the curve.

The yield curve steepened on Monday with the spread between two- and 10-year yields rising six basis points. The 10-year spread between French and German yields remained relatively stable at minus nine basis points.
